# Public Reproduction

Run from the task directory:

~~~bash
python reproduce.py
~~~

The offline study uses compact deterministic checkpoints instead of raw
scanner files. It exercises two normal high-level Osprey entrypoints:

- `edited_model` passes each prepared fit checkpoint through `OspreyFit`, so
  sequence selection remains owned by the candidate project;
- `quantitative_report` resumes each prepared post-fit checkpoint through
  `RunOspreyJob`, with already-completed acquisition stages replaced by
  deterministic offline shims.

The report is written to:

~~~text
outputs/reproduction_report.json
~~~

For each record it reports only externally inspectable workflow information:
the record identifier, the acquisition sequence where applicable, whether the
high-level stage completed, the number of numeric values returned by that
stage, and a finite aggregate norm. It does not name low-level dispatch
targets, select an internal quantitative field, reconstruct a correct result,
or apply a task-specific compatibility threshold.

Status meanings:

- `workflow_completed`: both high-level workflows returned non-empty, fully
  finite inspectable observations. Exit code `0`.
- `runner_failure`: a dependency or high-level workflow failed, returned an
  incomplete result, or produced a non-finite observation. Exit code `2`.

The JSON writer rejects `NaN` and infinity. `workflow_completed` is not a
public certificate that the repair is correct: both the supplied snapshot and
a scientifically repaired implementation may complete. Compare the reported
observations as part of the investigation; the private verifier evaluates the
scientific cross-protocol contracts over additional inputs.
# Repair inconsistent cross-protocol Osprey validation reports

A spectroscopy group is validating a historical Osprey snapshot with
deterministic checkpoints derived from one synthetic phantom study. All runs
complete and produce finite values, but two independent report panels are not
compatible across supported acquisition configurations:

- a model-derived contribution changes substantially between edited
  acquisition encodings that represent the same calibration;
- a downstream quantitative result changes substantially between acquisition
  settings prepared to represent the same control.

Run the public reproduction, inspect the project source, checkpoints, and data
structures, and repair the scientific
implementation. A valid repair must preserve legitimate dependence on sequence
design, basis content, fitted signals, acquisition metadata, field strength,
and supported correction models.

Do not hard-code the visible records, replace either report with a fixed value,
or edit generated outputs.

source/docs_source/04-tutorial.Rmd:130:The left panel shows the raw water-scaled metabolite estimates, i.e. the signal amplitudes normalized by the water amplitude. The amplitude parameters will subsequently be used during the quantification process to derive tCr ratios and water-scaled estimates.
source/docs_source/04-tutorial.Rmd:180:Below the overlay produced by `CoRegister`, you can now see four images showing the voxel mask next to the contributions from grey matter, white matter, and CSF, along with the fractional volume estimates for each tissue class. These values will subsequently be used during quantification to account for tissue-specific effects of relaxation, tissue water content, and metabolite content.
source/docs_source/04-tutorial.Rmd:186:## Quantification
source/docs_source/04-tutorial.Rmd:188:Click the `Quantify` button to have **Osprey** run the `OspreyQuantify` module in the background. This should take less than a second per dataset. During this process, several quantitative metabolite estimates are calculated, such as tCr ratios and water-scaled estimates with different degrees of sophistication. Please refer to the **Osprey** manuscript for details on the implementation of these quantification routines.
source/docs_source/04-tutorial.Rmd:190:Once the quantification is complete, the `Quantify` tab becomes active:
source/docs_source/04-tutorial.Rmd:196:This tab contains a bare-bone table of the quantitative results for each basis function and each quantification routine for the selected dataset. These numbers are saved in `.CSV` format tables in the `QuantifyResults` sub-directory of the output folder.
source/docs_source/04-tutorial.Rmd:202:After quantification is complete, another tab becomes active: `Overview`. This tab contains several visualizations that are interesting for the batched analysis of multiple datasets.
source/docs_source/04-tutorial.Rmd:232:- **Quantify table**: Shows a table with the results of a specific quantification routine for all metabolites and all datasets.
source/docs_source/04-tutorial.Rmd:235:You can select the quantification routine to be displayed (tCr ratios, raw water-scaled, CSF-corrected water-scaled, tissue-corrected water-scaled) by using the dropdown menu at the top of the window.
source/docs_source/04-tutorial.Rmd:242:- **Distribution**: Shows a raincloud plot of the results of a specific quantification routine for a specific metabolite. The raincloud plot includes a visualization of the distribution, the mean and median values of the distribution, standard deviation, and 25% and 75% percentiles. In addition, each data point is shown.
source/docs_source/04-tutorial.Rmd:245:You can select the quantification routine to be displayed (tCr ratios, raw water-scaled, CSF-corrected water-scaled, tissue-corrected water-scaled), as well as the particular metabolite you want to study.
source/docs_source/04-tutorial.Rmd:257:You can select the quantification routine and metabolite to be correlated, as well as another metabolite or quality metric that it is to be correlated against, by using the dropdown menus at the top of the window.
